distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "which made it an ideal platform for radio antennas" is a dependent clause.

distractorRationales.label: D
distractorRationales.text: A relative clause that adds nonessential information about a noun that is already identified ("its great height") must be set off with a comma.

passages.text: Urban planner Tomás Ferreira expected that new benches along a riverside walking path would mainly benefit older visitors. The benches turned out to be popular with nearly every age ______ teenagers were the group most often found sitting on them in the evenings.

content.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
content.explanation: "The benches turned out to be popular with nearly every age group" and "teenagers were the group most often found sitting on them in the evenings" are both independent clauses. The phrase "in fact" belongs with the second clause, because it introduces a stronger point that builds on the first (not only were the benches popular with all ages, but teenagers used them most). Two independent clauses joined by a transitional phrase need a semicolon before the phrase, and an introductory phrase like "in fact" is followed by a comma. So "group; in fact," is correct.

distractorRationales.label: A
distractorRationales.text: Commas alone cannot join two independent clauses. Putting "in fact" between commas still leaves a comma splice between "...every age group" and "teenagers were..."

distractorRationales.label: B
distractorRationales.text: The semicolon is correctly placed, but the introductory phrase "in fact" at the start of the second clause needs a comma after it.

distractorRationales.label: C
distractorRationales.text: The semicolon placed after "in fact" attaches the phrase to the first clause ("popular with nearly every age group in fact"), but "in fact" introduces the stronger point in the second clause. The semicolon belongs before "in fact."
